newsitem.title: FRANCE: Details of French government's tax reforms.
newsitem.headline: Details of French government's tax reforms.

text.p: The following gives details of tax reforms announced on Thursday by the French government.
INCOME TAX REDUCTION
Income taxes will be cut by 75 billion francs over five years, including 25 billion francs on taxes payable in 1997 on 1996 income.
The top rate of tax will be reduced to 54 percent next year from 56.8 percent and the reform aims to bring this top rate down to 47 percent within five years.
All income tax rates will be lowered and the threshhold before people have to start paying tax will be raised to help those on low incomes.
PAYROLL CHARGES AND THE CSG

Employee payroll contributions to cover healthcare will be reduced by 1.3 percentage points, which will be offset by an increase in the CSG (Generalised Social Contribution) to 3.4 percent from 2.4 percent. The CSG will be widened to cover virtually all income, including income from savings.
The additional one point increase in the CSG will be made tax deductible.
The increased tax burden to pay for the welfare system will total seven billion francs, meaning that the net tax cut next year will be 18 billion francs.
LIFE-ASSURANCE

Tax benefits given for contributions to new life assurance policies will be scrapped from September 5, 1996. Benefits on proceeds from life policies will not be touched, although these proceeds will in future pay the CSG tax.
Contributions previously agreed for existing life policies will continue to benefit from tax breaks.
PENSION FUNDS
France will introduce pension funds to complement the existing universal pension system. These will be set up by employers or groups of employers, but managed by independent specialists.
Workers will contribute on a voluntary basis and it will be up to the companies themselves to decide whether or not to top up their employees' contributions.
There will be no limits on allocation of assets by the pension funds, which will be free to make their own choices about how much to invest in stocks and bonds.
But prudential rules, which currently tend to disfavour investment in shares will be changed.
ABOLITION OF SPECIAL TAX DEDUCTIONS
Special tax deductions given to some 100 professions, including journalists, will be phased out over five years, starting with 1997 income, payable in 1998.
A 10 percent tax deduction for retired people will be progressively and significantly reduced.
Maternity benefits will be taxed, covering 1996 income onwards.

Tax deductions for people with children who are no longer of school age will be reduced significantly, while some tax breaks for those with children in secondary or tertiary education will be scrapped.
